edits.name: Equality of the quantum Jellium and uniform electron gas energies
edits.statement: Lieb and Narnhofer (1975) defined the ground-state energy per unit volume $e^\hbar_{\rm Jel}(\rho_0)$ of Jellium: electrons in a uniform neutralizing background of density $\rho_0$, with no constraint on their density. Lewin, Lieb and Seiringer defined the energy per unit volume $e^\hbar_{\rm UEG}(\rho_0)$ of the uniform electron gas: electrons whose density is constrained to equal $\rho_0$ everywhere, with no background. They called the question of whether the two coincide important for density functional theory, and wrote that the equality is expected in the quantum case. The classical case $\hbar=0$ was proved by Lewin, Lieb and Seiringer and by Cotar and Petrache. Is $e^\hbar_{\rm Jel}(\rho_0)=e^\hbar_{\rm UEG}(\rho_0)$ for every $\hbar>0$ and $\rho_0>0$?
edits.posedBy: Lewin, Lieb and Seiringer, Statistical mechanics of the uniform electron gas (J. Ec. polytech. Math. 2018); quantum case expected in The local density approximation in DFT (2020), Sec. 2.2
edits.ageNote: The 2018 paper (arXiv 2017) says it does not answer "the important question of whether Jellium and the UEG are the same". The classical case was settled in 2019; the 2020 paper says the same is expected in the quantum case.

edits.resultNote: Theorem 1: for every spin multiplicity $q\ge1$, every $\rho_0>0$ and every $\hbar>0$, the canonical Dirichlet Jellium energy of Lieb and Narnhofer equals the Lewin-Lieb-Seiringer UEG energy. Both inequalities are proved. Before this, only $e^\hbar_{\rm Jel}\le e^\hbar_{\rm UEG}$ was known, and only for a grand-canonical Jellium whose identification with the Lieb-Narnhofer energy had not been proved; the paper proves that inequality for the Lieb-Narnhofer energy too. The upper bound uses packed Dirichlet Jellium balls with compensated shells, not a floating crystal. Consequence: the known UEG properties (high-density expansion, classical limit) transfer to Jellium.

edits.significanceNote: A foundational question of the mathematical theory of the electron gas, raised by Lewin, Lieb and Seiringer and widely assumed by physicists; the classical case fell in 2019. Known well within mathematical physics and DFT, not beyond. Above Kohn-Sham ensemble v-representability (22), below the one-dimensional Lieb-Thirring conjecture (36) and the Sandier-Serfaty triangular-lattice conjecture (42).

edits.statement: The irrationality exponent of an irrational $x$ is $\mu(x)=\sup\{\nu>0:0<|x-p/q|<q^{-\nu}$ for infinitely many coprime integers $p,q$, $q\ge2\}$; Dirichlet gives $\mu(x)\ge2$ and almost every real has $\mu=2$. Upper bounds have been obtained for values $\arctan(1/n)$: Tomashevskaya (2008) gave a general estimate, Salikhov and Bashmakova (2020) improved the bounds for $\arctan(1/3)$ and $\arctan(1/5)$, and Bai (2026) reported $\mu(\arctan(1/2))\le 8.585166\ldots$. Since $\arctan 1=\pi/4$, the case $r=1$ is the conjecture $\mu(\pi)=2$. Is $\mu(\arctan r)=2$ for every nonzero rational $r$?
edits.resultNote: Claimed: for every nonzero rational $r$, $\mu(\arctan r)=2$, and for every rational $r>0$, $\mu(\sqrt r\,\pi)=2$. Both are corollaries of a quadratic field criterion: if $D$ is a nonsquare integer, $x\ne0$ real, and $e^{2\sqrt D x}\in\mathbb Q(\sqrt D)$ has norm one, then $\mu(x)=2$, with an ineffective threshold. For $D=-1$ and $x=\arctan r$, $e^{2ix}=(1+ir)/(1-ir)$. The case $r=1$ recovers the OpenAI release's $\mu(\pi)=2$, already a Candidate here; the method adapts that manuscript's determinant argument with the interpolation theorems of Liu, Jiang and Zhang (arXiv 2610.10192, $\mu(\log r)=2$).
edits.aiRole: The README and the preprint's AI declaration say GPT-6 Astra helped determine what follows from $\mu(\pi)=2$ and the Liu-Jiang-Zhang interpolation theorems, and built the Lean repository, the authors being new to Lean. Thank you for this, and for the care in the note about what is and is not claimed.

We read the Zenodo note, the Lean file, Mathematics Stack Exchange question 5151787 with Greg Martin's comment, the release's quasi-Riemann manuscript and our entries for it and for the least quadratic nonresidue. The deduction looks right to us, and Martin's public comment supports it: under the claimed $7/8$ half-plane, his Proposition 3 gives $g^*(p)\ll(\log p)^{24}$, which implies Vinogradov's conjecture.

Vinogradov's least primitive root conjecture is a landmark-tier claim, and the site has one rule for those: it lists them, as Candidates, once someone accountable stands behind them: named authors, a lab publishing under its own name, or a formal proof whose statement and axioms we can read. The note is by a pseudonymous author, and the Lean file does not prove the claim: it takes the $7/8$ statement as an uninterpreted proposition and Martin's estimate as a hypothesis, so it checks only the final few lines. Its header also says it was prepared without a Lean compiler and has not been compiled, which contradicts the Zenodo description; please reconcile the two.

So it is declined for now, as a scope decision and not a verdict on the mathematics. Resubmission is welcome when a named author signs the note, or when a lab or a refereed source records the corollary. If Greg Martin, or anyone named, writes it up under their own name, that would qualify at once.

edits.name: Eden's conjecture on the maximal local Lyapunov dimension
edits.statement: Let $\{\varphi^t\}_{t\geq 0}$ be a dynamical system on $\mathbb R^n$ with a global attractor $K$. Eden's conjecture states that the supremum of the local Lyapunov dimensions over $K$ is attained at a stationary point or on an unstable periodic orbit embedded in $K$. Is that true?
edits.posedBy: Alp Eden, PhD thesis (Indiana University, 1989), p. 98, Question 1; see also Eden, M2AN 23 (1989) 405-413
edits.ageNote: The literature (Wikipedia, Kuznetsov's surveys) dates the conjecture to 1987; the written source Kuznetsov cites is Eden's 1989 Indiana thesis, p. 98, Question 1. It was known to hold for the Lorenz system and the complex Ginzburg-Landau equation in some parameter ranges.
edits.aiRole: The repository README, under Credit: "Much of the counterexample construction was assisted by GPT-6 Astra. The authors independently searched the literature to verify the findings and discern the valid statements to use."
edits.resultNote:
A $C^1$ (polynomial) flow on $\mathbb R^5$ with a global attractor containing an invariant two-torus with an irrational flow, where the local Lyapunov dimension is $9/2$, while it is at most $3$ at every stationary point and on every periodic orbit. So the supremum is not attained at a stationary point or periodic orbit, with or without the word "unstable". The repository also refutes a version for strange (noninteger Hausdorff dimension) local attractors and the critical-path form of Eden's Question 1.

A concurrent independent counterexample, also AI-assisted and formalised in Lean, is Matthew Colbrook's "Aperiodic maximisers of Lyapunov dimension" (Zenodo, 21 September 2026): a polynomial system on $\mathbb R^5$ of dimension $4+4/c$ on a torus for every $c>4$. The repository's current construction, revised on 17 October, appears to be its case $c=8$; the September commits used a different setting.
edits.verificationNote: Read by this site on 3 November 2026 at commit 69547cb, not rebuilt; the repository has no CI. The headline statements in EdensConjecture/EStatements.lean and their definitions were read: a C1 flow on Euclidean space solving its ODE, a compact invariant set attracting every bounded subset of the phase domain, the local Lyapunov dimension as the infimum of orders with negative upper growth rate of the singular-value function, its supremum over the attractor, and instability as failure of orbital Lyapunov stability. In the global counterexample the phase domain is all of R^5, so the attractor is genuinely global. The proof gives local dimension 9/2 on the torus and at most 3 at every stationary or periodic point, and DefinitionCheck.lean proves the Kuznetsov-Reitmann and both Kaplan-Yorke definitions agree there. The EdensConjecture library has no sorry, admit, axiom declarations, native_decide, unsafe, implemented_by or opaque; sorry appears only in separate, unimported Kuznetsov-Eden files. The formal statement was written by the provers and is not anchored in Formal Conjectures or a tracker. Eden's thesis was not available here; the statement was compared with Kuznetsov (arXiv 1602.05410) and Wikipedia.
edits.significanceNote: A named conjecture from 1987 that has organised work on Lyapunov dimension estimates for decades (Leonov, Kuznetsov and coauthors), with a Wikipedia article, but known mainly inside that community. Level with the homogeneous polynomial Lyapunov conjecture and Carrasco's OZF conjecture at 15, below the Denjoy sharpness entry at 20 and the quintic Lienard entry at 25, which reach wider audiences.

edits.ageNote: Proposed by Pólya and Szegő (1951). Szegő's symmetrization proof (1950, corrected 1958) needs a first eigenfunction of one sign, which cannot be assumed. Known before: the nonsharp Bramble-Payne bound $|\Omega|\Lambda_1>2\pi j_{0,1}^2$ and existence of optimal domains (Ashbaugh-Bucur 2003, Stollenwerk 2023). Listed as open in Colbrook's AIM catalogue, Problem 007, last checked 8 September 2026.
edits.resultNote: The authors prove the planar Pólya-Szegő conjecture for every open set $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^2$ of finite positive area, without assumptions on connectedness, boundedness, boundary regularity or the sign of an eigenfunction: $|\Omega|\Lambda_1(\Omega)\geq\pi j_{1,1}^2$, with equality if and only if $\Omega$ is an open disk. The route is a new sharp buckling-Dirichlet comparison $\Lambda_1(\Omega)\geq (j_{1,1}^2/j_{0,1}^2)\lambda_1^{\mathrm D}(\Omega)$ combined with Faber-Krahn, and the disk formula $\Lambda_1(B_R)=j_{1,1}^2/R^2$. All five statements are formalized in Lean 4 and registered at Palomar (PALOMAR-2026-10-18-000008). The informal manuscript is a working draft (v5, 18 October 2026) in the repository, not yet on arXiv. Dimensions $N\geq3$ remain open.

edits.statement: For $g\geq 2$ let $\mathrm{Sys}(g)$ be the supremum of the systoles of closed oriented hyperbolic surfaces of genus $g$. edits.ageNote: No poser recorded: a standing asymptotic question rather than a posed conjecture. edits.statement: For a weakly increasing $h:[n]\to[n]$ with $i\le h(i)$, the natural unit interval graph $G$ on $[n]$ has edges $\{i,j\}$ with $i<j\le h(i)$. Its chromatic quasisymmetric function is $X_G(x;q)=\sum_\kappa q^{\mathrm{asc}(\kappa)}x_\kappa$, summed over proper colorings, where $\mathrm{asc}(\kappa)$ counts edges $i<j$ with $\kappa(i)<\kappa(j)$; Shareshian and Wachs proved it symmetric and palindromic in $q$. Write $X_G=\sum_{j=0}^{m}a_j(x)q^j$ with $m=|E(G)|$. Conjecture 1.3 asserts that each $a_j$ is $e$-positive and that $a_{j+1}-a_j$ is $e$-positive for $0\le j<(m-1)/2$; equivalently, every coefficient $c_{G,\lambda}(q)$ of $e_\lambda$ is a nonnegative, palindromic, unimodal polynomial. Is this true for every natural unit interval graph?
edits.posedBy: John Shareshian and Michelle L. Wachs, Chromatic quasisymmetric functions, Conjecture 1.3 (arXiv:1405.4629; Adv. Math. 295 (2016), 497-551)
edits.ageNote: Conjecture 1.3 of arXiv:1405.4629 (2014; Adv. Math. 2016) states positivity and unimodality together. The catalog's positivity entry dates the conjecture to the 2012 CRM paper (arXiv 1106.4287); that dating was not rechecked here. Unimodality was known before only for families: Cho-Huh, abelian Hessenberg graphs, melting lollipops, K-chains.
edits.resultNote: Theorem 1.1: for every natural unit interval graph $G$ with $e$ edges and every $\lambda\vdash|V(G)|$, $c_{G,\lambda}(q)=\sum_{j=0}^{\lfloor e/2\rfloor}a_{G,\lambda,j}q^j(1+q+\cdots+q^{e-2j})$ with $a_{G,\lambda,j}\in\mathbb N$, so every elementary coefficient is nonnegative, palindromic about $e/2$ and unimodal. With positivity this is the whole of Conjecture 1.3. The proof builds rigid quiver potentials with nilpotent Jacobian algebras and uses purity and hard Lefschetz for BPS sheaves. It inherits the triangular charts, rotations and section formalism of OpenAI's unrefereed September 2026 positivity manuscript (its Sections 2 and 4-5, not its positivity proof in Section 3), so it depends on that framework. Log-concavity, which is stronger, fails in general.
edits.verificationNote: No independent mathematician has checked this yet. Read by this site on 3 November 2026. The Zenodo record (v1, 22 October 2026, sole author Mingchang Liu, 31 pages) was opened; Theorem 1.1 was read against Conjecture 1.3 in the arXiv version of Shareshian-Wachs and states it in full, given the known palindromicity. The AI statement is in the manuscript. A separate computation written here expanded $X_G$ in the elementary basis for all 132 natural unit interval graphs on up to 6 vertices (1,836 coefficients) and found every coefficient nonnegative, palindromic and unimodal; it says nothing about larger graphs. The proof was not read, and its dependence on the unrefereed OpenAI framework was not assessed.

edits.statement: Let $p$ be a prime, $n=2^k$ with $k\ge0$, $F=\mathbb F_{p^n}$, and $\psi$ the canonical additive character of $F$. For a positive integer $d$ with $\gcd(d,p^n-1)=1$, put $W_d(a)=\sum_{x\in F}\psi(x^d-ax)$. Helleseth conjectured that the spectrum $\{W_d(a):a\in F^\times\}$ never has exactly three distinct values; equivalently, the cross-correlation of a $p$-ary m-sequence of period $p^n-1$ with its $d$-decimation is never three-valued. Is that true?

edits.statement: Does Yudovich's uniqueness theorem extend below bounded vorticity? For the unforced two-dimensional incompressible Euler equations, is a weak solution with vorticity in $L^\infty_t L^p_x$, $p<\infty$, uniquely determined by its initial vorticity, in particular for large $p$? Bruè, Colombo and Kumar call this a central question (on $\mathbb{T}^2$, with velocity in $L^2$); without force it was open for every $p$ beyond the small $p>1$ reached by their convex integration.

edits.resultNote:
Theorem A: a positive integer $k$ equals $|\mathcal D(X)|$ for some metric continuum $X$ if and only if $k\notin\{2,4,5,8,9,16\}$. This settles Problem 4.14 (Question 3.5) and answers Question 3.21 positively: every $k\ge17$ occurs. Also, $|\mathcal D(X)|=2^m$ exactly when $m=0$ or $m\ge5$ (Pregunta 3.1.13).

The finite values are exactly the numbers of connected vertex sets of finite connected graphs, each graph realized by Knaster continua glued at points. A recursive family realizes every $k\ge17$ on $\lfloor\log_2 k\rfloor+1$ vertices (six for $k=25$), the least possible for $k\ge32$. Context: Czabarka, Székely and Wagner (2009) had shown that every integer from $90$ on is the number of subtrees of a tree, so with a realization of trees the values $k\ge90$ followed from earlier work, as the paper says; the new parts are the realization for all graphs, the computer-free determination and the least-vertex result.

edits.statement: Tuza's conjecture (1981) asks whether every finite simple graph $G$ satisfies $\tau_\triangle(G)\leq2\nu_\triangle(G)$, where $\tau_\triangle$ is the minimum number of edges meeting every triangle and $\nu_\triangle$ is the maximum number of edge-disjoint triangles. This entry concerns the split graphs in which the vertices of $I$ with at least two neighbours in $C$ have at most two distinct neighbourhoods in $C$. Zeng (2026) settled this case when $|C|=8$. Does the inequality hold for every clique size and every multiplicity?

edits.name: Polynomial-time Hamiltonian s-t paths in solid grid graphs
edits.shortName: Hamiltonian paths in solid grid graphs
edits.field: Algorithmic graph theory; Hamiltonian paths in grid graphs
edits.statement: A grid graph is a finite set $V\subset\mathbb Z^2$ with an edge between every two points at distance $1$; it is solid if it has no holes. Itai, Papadimitriou and Szwarcfiter (1982) showed that deciding whether a grid graph has a Hamiltonian path between given vertices $s$ and $t$ is NP-complete, and that it is solvable in linear time for rectangular grid graphs. Umans and Lenhart (1997) gave a polynomial-time algorithm for Hamiltonian cycles in solid grid graphs. Is there a polynomial-time algorithm that decides, for a solid grid graph $V$ and distinct $s,t\in V$, whether $V$ has a Hamiltonian path from $s$ to $t$?
edits.posedBy: Implicit in Itai, Papadimitriou and Szwarcfiter (SIAM J. Comput. 1982), who asked the hole-free question for cycles; the path case is stated open later, e.g. by Keshavarz-Kohjerdi and Bagheri (2016).
edits.ageNote: Itai, Papadimitriou and Szwarcfiter (1982) settled general and rectangular grid graphs and left open the hole-free case in its cycle form, which Umans and Lenhart answered in 1997. The path form has been cited as open since; the earliest explicit statement of it read here is from 2016.
edits.aiRole: According to the repository README, Claude (Opus 5.5) did nearly all of the work: the algorithm, the paper, reference implementations in C, Python and JavaScript, the browser demo and the Lean 4 proof. The human author, zzyzek, supplied the problem statement and guidance.

edits.name: The Exponential Time Hypothesis
edits.statement: For $k\ge3$ let $s_k$ be the infimum of the $\delta$ for which $k$-SAT on $n$ variables can be decided in time $O(2^{\delta n})$. Impagliazzo and Paturi (2001) formulated the Exponential Time Hypothesis: $s_3>0$, that is, there is a $\delta>0$ such that $3$-SAT cannot be solved in time $2^{\delta n}$, so no $2^{o(n)}$-time algorithm exists. With the sparsification lemma of Impagliazzo, Paturi and Zane (2001) it underlies tight conditional lower bounds across exact, parameterized and fine-grained complexity, and it is a strengthening of $\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}$. Is it true?
edits.posedBy: Russell Impagliazzo and Ramamohan Paturi, On the Complexity of k-SAT, J. Comput. Syst. Sci. 62(2) (2001)
edits.ageNote: Year from the manuscript's reference [IP01] (J. Comput. Syst. Sci. 62(2), 2001, 367-375); the sparsification companion [IPZ01] is the same year.
edits.aiRole: Produced by an unreleased internal OpenAI model as part of an OpenAI evaluation on open research problems. The manuscript is authored 'OpenAI' and names no human author. The release README says the manuscripts are best understood as raw research data rather than polished papers, and that unformalized results could have issues. The manuscript is dated 17 October 2026, revised 25 October 2026; OpenAI's announcement says the model found the disproof on 16 October and that it was checked in Lean the next day. The release history (26 October) says an independent working group led by Russell Impagliazzo, Ramamohan Paturi and Ryan Williams will examine and explain the proof, and that the materials were made public at the group's request. The release ships a Lean formalization and a Comparator configuration for the main theorem.
edits.resultNote: Theorem 1.1: for each fixed $k\ge2$ a deterministic algorithm computes the number of satisfying assignments of a $k$-CNF with $n\ge20$ variables and $m$ clauses in $(n+m)^{O_k(1)}2^{O_k(n\log\log n/\sqrt{\log n})}$ bit operations and $(n+m)^{O_k(1)}$ bits of space, and in $2^{O_{k,D}(n/\sqrt{\log n})}$ when $m\le Dn$. Testing whether the count is positive decides $3$-SAT in $2^{o(n)}$ time, refuting ETH (and hence SETH). The paper notes this does not give subexponential algorithms for all of NP, since $2^{o(n)}$ bounds do not survive general polynomial reductions. Corollaries: subexponential Max-$k$-SAT approximation schemes, exact counting of independent sets, $q$-colorings and perfect matchings in $2^{o(v)}$ time, and an $\Omega(n\log n)$ circuit lower bound for a language in $E^{NP}$.
edits.verificationNote: No independent mathematician has checked this yet. Checked here on 3 November 2026: the abstract, introduction and Theorem 1.1, read against ETH as defined in [IP01]. The proof was not refereed. Lean: lean/formalization.yaml lists OAI.Algorithms.SubexponentialSAT.SqrtLogSpace.exact_count_and_sat (SqrtLogSpace/Final.lean, comparator ComparatorChallenges/SubexponentialSAT.json, axioms propext, Quot.sound, Classical.choice). Its challenge statement was read in full: for each $k\ge2$ one fixed multi-tape machine over Mathlib Turing tapes, on a canonical unary-coded CNF of bit length $L$, halts with the exact count and the SAT bit, in time at most $C(L+1)^d2^{A\,n(\log\log n)^2/\sqrt{\log n}}$ and visited space at most $S(L+1)^e$. A 3-CNF has $L=\mathrm{poly}(n)$, so this is a $2^{o(n)}$ deterministic 3-SAT algorithm: the headline, with no extra hypotheses, at a slightly weaker exponent than the paper's. GitHub code search over the solution folder found no sorry, native_decide or implemented_by, and only #print axioms lines for 'axiom'; the search does not index every one of its about 4,000 files. Not rebuilt here.
edits.significanceNote: ETH (Impagliazzo-Paturi 2001) is the basic hardness hypothesis of exact and fine-grained complexity, a strengthening of P vs NP that thousands of conditional lower bounds rest on, and it was almost universally believed. Placed above the Unique Games Conjecture (74), the other central TCS hypothesis of the same era, and far above the APSP hypothesis (55) and the 3SUM hypothesis (50), the other fine-grained pillars; below the BSD formula entry (78) and the Navier-Stokes Millennium entry (87).

edits.name: Sogge's local smoothing conjecture for the wave equation in every dimension
edits.field: Harmonic analysis; dispersive and wave equations
edits.statement: For the half-wave propagator $e^{it\sqrt{-\Delta}}$ on $\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$, the sharp fixed-time estimate on $L^p$ loses $(n-1)|1/2-1/p|$ derivatives. Sogge (1991) conjectured that averaging over $t\in[1,2]$ gains almost $1/p$ of a derivative: $\|e^{it\sqrt{-\Delta}}f\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n\times[1,2])}\le C\|f\|_{W^{\sigma,p}}$ for every $\sigma>(n-1)(1/2-1/p)-1/p$ when $p\ge 2n/(n-1)$, and every $\sigma>0$ when $2<p\le 2n/(n-1)$. The conjecture implies the Bochner-Riesz conjecture and, through it, the Fourier restriction and Kakeya conjectures. It was proved for $n=2$ by Guth, Wang and Zhang; in higher dimensions Bourgain-Demeter decoupling gave $p\ge2(n+1)/(n-1)$. Does it hold in every dimension?
edits.posedBy: Christopher D. Sogge, Propagation of singularities and maximal functions in the plane, Invent. Math. 104 (1991)
edits.ageNote: The manuscript cites Sogge 1991 [72, Section 4, Equation (4.5)] as the source of the question.
edits.aiRole: Produced by an unreleased internal OpenAI model as part of an OpenAI evaluation on open research problems. The manuscript is authored 'OpenAI' and names no human author. The release README says the manuscripts are best understood as raw research data rather than polished papers, and that unformalized results could have issues. The release history (26 October 2026) says OpenAI is releasing this model output directly, as in its 6 October release, and that the proof uses an auxiliary partial differential equation; OpenAI's announcement says the model produced it on 18 October. It extends the release's 24 September three-dimensional result (catalogued as local-smoothing-conjecture-r3) to every dimension. Lean formalizations and a Comparator configuration ship for the headline theorem and five consequences.
edits.resultNote: Theorem 1.1: for $n\ge2$, $2\le p<\infty$ and $\varepsilon>0$, $\|e^{-iT|D|}f\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n\times[1,2])}\le C\|J^{s_+(p)+\varepsilon}f\|_{L^p}$ with $s_+(p)=\max\{0,(n-1)/2-n/p\}$, and $\varepsilon=0$ at $p=2$: Sogge's conjecture in its strict form in every dimension. Consequences in the paper: the Bochner-Riesz conjecture for $1\le p\le\infty$ with maximal bounds, Stein's square function, global sphere and truncated-cone extension estimates in the interior of the conjectured range, the compact paraboloid and Schrodinger local smoothing, and the Kakeya and Nikodym maximal conjectures, so every Kakeya set in $\mathbb R^n$ has Hausdorff dimension $n$. Not shown: the endpoint $\sigma=0$ at $p\ge 2n/(n-1)$ or restriction endpoints. It supersedes the catalog's three-dimensional entry.
edits.verificationNote: No independent mathematician has checked this yet. Checked here on 3 November 2026: the abstract, Section 1 and Theorem 1.1 were read against Sogge's conjecture; the exponent $\max\{0,(n-1)/2-n/p\}$ equals the conjectured $(n-1)(1/2-1/p)-1/p$ above $2n/(n-1)$ and $0$ below. The proof was not refereed. Lean: formalization.yaml lists six declarations under OAI.Analysis.Fourier.LocalSmoothing.Comparator (comparator ComparatorChallenges/LocalSmoothing.json, axioms propext, Quot.sound, Classical.choice). The challenge file was read in full: euclidean_local_smoothing states, for every $n\ge2$, $p\ge2$ and $\varepsilon>0$ (or $p=2$, $\varepsilon=0$), the $L^p(\mathbb R^n\times[1,2])$ bound by the Bessel-potential norm of order $\max(0,(n-1)/2-n/p)+\varepsilon$ for Schwartz data, with Fourier transforms defined from scratch; the other five (Bochner-Riesz for all $\delta>\max(n|1/p-1/2|-1/2,0)$, spherical extension, Kakeya maximal with $\delta^{-\varepsilon}$ loss, $\dim_H F=n$ for every Kakeya set, Stein square function) match the paper's statements. GitHub code search of the solution folder found no sorry, axiom or native_decide. Not rebuilt here.
edits.significanceNote: Sogge's 1991 conjecture sits at the top of the Euclidean harmonic analysis hierarchy: in every dimension it implies Bochner-Riesz, restriction and Kakeya, the last itself among the most famous open problems in analysis. Placed well above its own three-dimensional case (63) and the four-dimensional Kakeya set conjecture (55), level with the Landau-Siegel zeros entry (72), below the Unique Games Conjecture (74), a hypothesis known across all of theoretical computer science.
